summary: Prukalpa Sankar frames the core problem: models are exponentially smarter but not proportionally more useful, because performance depends on both intelligence and context. Only 10% of job performance variance is explained by IQ; the rest is contextual knowledge, expertise, and norms learned on the job. Models have 1000x'd in intelligence over a decade while business context remains trapped in dashboards, Slack threads, and employees' heads. She illustrates this with Maya, a data analyst at Mac Context Burgers, who answers a seemingly simple question (why is drive-thru time up?) by applying facts, expertise, and norms learned through shadowing, mistakes, and feedback—not training manuals. Atlan's first era involved bootstrapping individual single-purpose agents (Hermione, MoneyPenny) via jobs-to-be-done analysis. This hit multiple walls: context engineering was slow, agents operated as isolated islands with no shared infrastructure, tracing failures was difficult, context sprawl meant each agent learned separately, and tech stack churn (Relevance, Google ADK, Glean, Claude Code, Codex) trapped context inside each system. The second era embraced general-purpose agents supported by a shared context layer—a company brain where domain skills accumulate. Atlan built 300 skills and 40 agents in six months, but discovered context must be managed like code: dependency management broke when skills evolved (competitive intel feeds category positioning feeds sales battle cards), skills drifted, ownership was unclear, and security was a nightmare with hardcoded secrets. The context layer concept—'GitHub for context'—requires lifecycle management, versioning, dependency tracking, approver/maintainer/contributor models, self-learning loops via traces, and multiple retrieval methods (MCP, SQL, vector, hybrid). Starting involves reverse-constructing connections between business systems (Salesforce, HubSpot, data warehouse, application layer) where context gets lost at every hop. Prukalpa concludes that today's hardcoding of context is unsustainable and dangerous at scale, and that context is IP: when competitors share the same models, what differentiates companies is how they encode their culture, norms, and business expertise into autonomous frontier firms.

sections.title: Introduction: Context Is King
sections.summary: Prukalpa introduces Atlan's mission—AI doesn't know your business, we fix that—and references Bill Gates' 'content is king' to argue context will be king in the agentic era.

sections.title: The Reality Distortion Field: Smarter Models, Stalled Utility
sections.summary: Models are exponentially smarter (top 1% bar exam scorers) yet not more useful: only 1 in 5 AI use cases reach production, 56% of CEOs see zero financial benefit.

sections.title: Performance = Intelligence + Context
sections.summary: Only 10% of job performance variance is explained by IQ. Intelligence has 1000x'd; context—situated business knowledge—has barely moved, remaining in dashboards, Slack, and employees' heads.

sections.title: The Human Learning Model: Maya at Mac Context Burgers
sections.summary: Maya, a data analyst, answers 'why is drive-thru time up?' by applying knowledge (definitions, time zones), expertise (seasonality, product launches), and norms (who's asking). She learned via shadowing, mistakes, and feedback—not training.

sections.title: Era One: Bootstrapping Individual Agents
sections.summary: Atlan's first approach used jobs-to-be-done analysis to build single-purpose agents (Hermione, MoneyPenny). Building agents was fast but context engineering was slow and quality-dependent, causing trust issues.

sections.title: Challenges of Isolated Agent Systems
sections.summary: Agents lived on islands: marketing changed positioning but the SDR agent pitched the old version. Failures were hard to trace. Context sprawl meant each agent learned separately. Tech stack churn (Relevance → Google ADK → Glean → Claude Code → Codex) trapped context in each system.

sections.title: Era Two: General-Purpose Agents and the Context Layer
sections.summary: Inspired by human dream teams with shared language, playbooks, and compounding memory, Atlan pivoted to general-purpose agents backed by a shared context layer—a company brain with retrieval mechanisms serving any agent.

sections.title: Marketing Team Case Study: Open Agent Block
sections.summary: The marketing team connected data, social, ad, and analytics systems to an open agent block supporting Claude Code, Co-work, and a custom Slack-based claw. Best domain experts built skills (SEO, competitive intel) into a common repo—a living brain with data graph, library of skills, semantics, metrics, and org structure.

sections.title: Challenges: Context Must Be Managed Like Code
sections.summary: With 300 skills and 40 agents in 6 months, Atlan hit new problems. Dependency management broke when skills evolved upstream (competitive intel → category positioning → sales battle cards). Skills drifted and became outdated. Skill quality ownership was unclear. Security was a nightmare: secrets hardcoded in .env files, people downloading public skill repos.

sections.title: Defining the Context Layer: The GitHub for Context
sections.summary: Prukalpa defines the context layer as 'GitHub for context': lifecycle management, collaboration, versioning, local vs. global context, skills with profiles and self-learning loops, quality and security posture management, and human-plus-AI workspaces with approvers, maintainers, and contributors.

sections.title: Compounding Learning Loops and Traces
sections.summary: Every AI interaction creates more context. Atlan deploys AI to read through agent traces, reverse-construct learnings, and feed them back into a maintainer loop as approve/reject/improve signals—creating a compounding learning loop.

sections.title: How to Start: Reverse-Constructing Business Systems
sections.summary: Starting is hard with 60+ disparate systems. Context is hidden in business systems and lost at every hop (Salesforce → HubSpot → warehouse → app layer). Reverse-constructing those connections and deploying AI on top yields an accurate first version of the company brain.

sections.title: Context Layer Architecture and Conclusion: Context Is IP
sections.summary: The context layer continually mines context from business systems, feeds it into a company brain, deploys via skills and context development life cycles, and retrieves via MCP, SQL, vector, and hybrid assembly. Hardcoding context is unsustainable at scale. Prukalpa concludes: context is IP. When competitors share the same models, differentiation comes from encoding culture and norms into autonomous frontier firms.

limitations: Single-purpose agents led to context engineering being slow and quality-dependent, causing trust issues with stakeholders.
Isolated agents could not share updates (e.g., marketing positioning changes not propagating to SDR agent).
Tracing failures back to model, agent, or context was difficult with isolated agent architectures.
Context sprawl: each agent had its own memory system and learned separately, preventing a single version of truth.
Changing agent frameworks trapped context inside each individual system.
Dependency management breaks when skills learn and evolve: upstream changes (e.g., competitive intel) break downstream skills (e.g., sales battle cards).
Skills quickly become outdated and drift without active lifecycle management.
Unclear ownership of skill quality—no one is accountable for maintaining skill accuracy.
Security and governance nightmare: secrets hardcoded in .env files, people downloading public skill repos.
Context lost at every hop between business systems (Salesforce → warehouse → app layer), degrading accuracy.
Hardcoding context into agents is unsustainable and dangerous at scale.
